title: Content-Based Filtering
summary: Recommend from item features and a user's own history alone — no other users' data required, and no filter-bubble-free lunch either.

slides.markdown:
Content-based filtering represents every item as a **feature vector** — structured attributes (genre, price, brand), tags, or a text/image embedding of its description. A movie might be `[genre: sci-fi, director: Nolan, runtime: 148, embedding: ...]`.

Once items live in a shared feature space, "similar item" becomes a geometric question: compute a distance or cosine similarity between vectors. This is the whole trick — recommendation reduces to nearest-neighbor search over item vectors, which is why it's often the simplest recommender to ship first.

To recommend for a user, build a **user profile vector** — typically the average (or weighted average, favoring recent activity) of the feature vectors of items they've liked. Then rank all candidate items by similarity to that profile.

Liked three dark psychological thrillers in a row? The profile vector sits in "thriller" space, so the next recommendation is another thriller — no other user's data was ever consulted. This is entirely self-contained per user, which is both the strength (works with zero other users) and the limitation (never learns from anyone else's taste).

For text-heavy items (articles, product descriptions, job listings), the feature vector is usually **TF-IDF** or a learned **embedding** (from a model like word2vec or a sentence transformer). Cosine similarity between two TF-IDF or embedding vectors stands in for "how similar are these two pieces of text."

Embeddings generally beat TF-IDF for this because they capture meaning, not just shared words — "laptop" and "notebook computer" land close together in embedding space even with zero overlapping tokens.

Pure content-based filtering **over-narrows**. Because it only ever recommends things similar to what you already liked, it has no mechanism for surfacing anything genuinely new — you liked thrillers, so you get thrillers forever, and the catalog's romance and documentary sections might as well not exist for you.

This is the classic **filter bubble**: recommendations that are locally accurate but globally boring, with zero serendipity. There's no cross-user signal at all to say "people like you, who also loved thrillers, unexpectedly loved this one documentary" — that leap requires collaborative signal, which content-based filtering structurally can't provide.

| | Content-based | Collaborative filtering |
|---|---|---|
| Needs other users? | No | Yes |
| New-item cold start | Solved (uses item's own features) | Broken (no interactions yet) |
| New-user cold start | Still broken (needs the user's own history) | Still broken |
| Serendipity | Low (filter bubble) | Higher (cross-user patterns) |

**How to decide:** content-based filtering solves new-item cold start but not new-user cold start — it needs *a* history to work from, just not anyone else's. That's exactly the gap collaborative filtering fills, which is why production systems combine both rather than picking one.
